title.en: The Creation: Ymir, Audhumla, and the World from a Giant's Body
title.zh: 北歐創世：尤彌爾、歐德姆布拉與巨人屍身造世

region.en: Ginnungagap (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland — provenance of Codex Regius)
region.zh: 金倫加鴻溝（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利——《雷吉烏斯抄本》產地）

texts.period: Poetic Edda poems c. 900-1000 CE (oral); Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda c. 1220-1230; principal MSS: Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to (c. 1270s, Iceland); Codex Upsaliensis DG 11 4to (c. 1300-1325)

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Gylfaginning 1-9 (trans. Anthony Faulkes, London, 1987); Voluspa 1-19, Codex Regius

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; eddic poems); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: In the yawning gap between ice and fire, the rime-giant Ymir is milked by the cow Audhumla, which licks forth Buri; Odin, Vili, and Ve kill Ymir and build the world from his body — earth from flesh, sea from blood, sky from skull — then create the first humans from two trees and set the world-tree Yggdrasil at the center.
summary.zh: 冰火之間的金倫加鴻溝中，霜巨人尤彌爾由母牛歐德姆布拉哺育，牛舔出布里；奧丁、維利與偉殺尤彌爾，以其屍造世——肉為地、血為海、顱骨為天；再以二木造最初人類，立世界樹尤克特拉希爾於宇宙之中心。

sensitivity.note: Historical literary corpus; occasionally claimed by modern heathen (Asatru) communities as heritage. Nothing restricted is reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gylfaginning 4-5: In Ginnungagap, where the icy rivers of Niflheim meet Muspell's heat, the rime took life as Ymir; the cow Audhumla licked the salt stones, and on the third day Buri came forth; Bor's sons — Odin, Vili, Ve — killed Ymir, and so much blood flowed that all his giant-kin drowned except Bergelmir, who escaped with his household on a raft. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gylfaginning 4-5; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gylfaginning 8: They took Ymir's skull and made the sky, setting it over the earth with its four corners held by dwarfs named East, West, North, South; his brains became the clouds; they took sparks from Muspell and set them in the heavens as stars, and built Midgard as a wall around the middle world against the giants. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gylfaginning 8; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Anthony Faulkes, Snorri Sturluson: Edda, Everyman, London 1987 (critical edition; excerpts public-domain via Brodeur 1916)

narrative.en:
The fullest account is Snorri Sturluson's Gylfaginning ('The Deluding of Gylfi'), framed as the Swedish king Gylfi's visit to Asgard, where three enthroned beings — High, Just-as-High, and Third — answer his questions about the world's origins, giving Snorri a question-and-answer platform for the learned paganism of Iceland.

BEGINNING: ICE, FIRE, AND THE FIRST GIANT. Before earth, sea, or heaven there was only Ginnungagap, the yawning void. To the north lay Niflheimr, world of mist and ice, whose spring Hvergelmir poured the icy rivers Elyagar; where the rivers met the void, the flowing venom hardened into rime, layer on layer. To the south burned Muspell, world of fire guarded by Surt with his flaming sword. Where the ice met Muspell's heat, the rime-drops took life: Ymir, the first rime-giant, ancestor of the hrimthursar. As Ymir slept in the melting ice, sweat from his left armpit bore a male and female giant, and one leg fathered a son with the other — the monsters breed without pairing. With him, the ice also formed the cow Audhumla, whose four rivers of milk fed Ymir; she herself licked the salty rime-stones, and by the first day a man's hair appeared, by the second a head, by the third a whole man — Buri, grandfather of the gods. Buri's son Bor married Bestla, a giant's daughter, and their three sons are Odin, Vili, and Ve — the gods, sprung from both divine and giant lines.

MIDDLE: THE SLAYING AND THE WORLD. The brothers slew Ymir — 'so much blood flowed from his wounds that with it they drowned all the race of the rime-giants, save one who escaped with his household: the giants call him Bergelmir', who built a raft (lutr) for himself and his wife and from them descends the race of giants (a flood-narrative embedded in the creation; the Voluspa 29 knows it in briefer form). Then Odin and his brothers carried Ymir to Ginnungagap and built the world from his body: his flesh became the earth; his blood the sea and lakes; his bones the mountains; his teeth and jaw-fragments the stones and cliffs; his skull they raised as the sky over the earth, setting dwarfs at its four corners — Austri, Vestri, Nordri, Sudri — to hold it; his brains became the clouds. Sparks from Muspell they fixed under the skull as stars, giving seats to some to light the world. Around the middle world they ringed Ymir's eyebrows into a fortress-wall against the hostile giants, and named that enclosure Midgard. One day, walking the sea-shore, the brothers found two trees (askr and embla, ash and elm — or 'man and woman' in some readings); Odin gave them breath and life, Vili gave them wit and motion, Ve gave form, speech, hearing, and sight — the first man and woman, Ask and Embla, within the wall of Midgard.

END: THE ORDERED COSMOS. Snorri then lays out the finished world: Yggdrasil, the world-ash, at the center, with three roots — one to the Aesir at Urðarbrunnr (the well of fate, where the Norns Urðr, Verðandi, and Skuld water it and mark each being's doom), one to Jotunheim at Mimir's well, where Odin pawned his eye for wisdom, and one to Niflheim above Hvergelmir, where the serpent Nidhoggr gnaws it. The rainbow-bridge Bifrost joins Asgard to Midgard, its red glow the burning air of the gods' fortress. The Aesir seat themselves at Ithavoll, and (Voluspa 8) 'in their courts they played at tables, no lack of gold' — the golden age before the first war (the Aesir-Vanir war, Voluspa 21-26) and the first killing. Snorri closes Gylfaginning 9 with the gods' genealogy down to Odin's sons, grounding the human dynasties of Snorri's separate historical work (Ynglinga saga, where the gods are euhemerized as ancient kings).

FUNCTIONS. The myth organizes the heathen cosmos into named places (Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Niflheim, Muspell) crossed by structuring elements (Yggdrasil, Bifrost, the rivers), explains human origin (trees, three gifts), the enmity of gods and giants (Bergelmir's survival), wisdom's price (Odin's eye), and time's order (the Norns); it legitimates Icelandic learning as memory of a system at risk of being lost — Snorri's stated purpose, to teach skalds the old kennings without letting the stories be forgotten.
narrative.zh: 太初唯金倫加鴻溝：北為霧之國尼福爾海姆，冰河注毒霜；南為火之國穆斯貝爾海姆。霜融而生尤彌爾，其腋出汗生男女巨人，足亦生子；冰復化母牛歐德姆布拉哺之，牛舔鹽石，三日舐出布里。布里之子博爾娶巨人女貝斯特拉，生奧丁、維利、偉三兄弟。三神誅尤彌爾，血流成災，巨人族唯伯格爾米爾夫婦乘筏得脫，後世巨人皆其苗裔。遂以屍造世：肉為大地，血為江海，骨為山嶽，齒牙為岩崖，顱骨為蒼穹，四方矮人承之，腦髓為雲，穆斯貝爾海姆火星為星。於世界中央以眉骨築牆，環圍中庭米德加爾特以拒巨人；海濱拾二木，奧丁賜氣息生命，維利賜智慧行動，偉賦形貌言語聽視——是為初人阿斯克與恩布拉。後立世界樹尤克特拉希爾，三根通神國、巨人國與霧國；命運三女神澆樹定命，奧丁以一目換密米爾井之智；彩虹橋畢弗羅斯特連神域與人域。諸神居伊達平原，擲金為戲，黃金時代始。功能：為異教宇宙命名分域、釋人類之起源、立神人仇怨之由、並記智慧之代價與時間之序。

functions: Cartography of the heathen cosmos: named worlds joined by Yggdrasil and Bifrost
Aition of human origin (Ask and Embla, three divine gifts) and of god-giant enmity
Wisdom economics: Odin's pawned eye at Mimir's well as the price of knowledge
Icelandic learned memory: Snorri's frame as skaldic preservation of a dying system

variants.name: Voluspa (Poetic Edda)
variants.text_tradition: Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270s (poem itself c. 900-1000 CE)
variants.summary: The sibyl's vision knows Ymir and the giants (st. 3: 'long ago... Ymir made; there was no sand, no sea, no cool waves'), but has no Audhumla, no cows, no dismemberment details; the killing is told in six lines ('all the gods slew Ymir...'), and Ask and Embla are given souls by three gods unnamed here as Odin, Hoenir, Loðurr (st. 18).

variants.name: Vafthrudnismal (Poetic Edda)
variants.summary: In the giant Vafthrudnir's answers, Bergelmir's raft (st. 35) is confirmed ('on a lut (lutr) they floated'), Ymir's blood became the sea (st. 28, 31), and the earliest ages are genealogized — the poem Snorri evidently mined for Gylfaginning.

variants.name: Grimnismal cosmology (Poetic Edda)
variants.summary: Odin in disguise recites the cosmology to a torturing king: Yggdrasil's three roots and their wells (st. 31), the named rivers, the halls of the gods, and the twelve worlds — a litany rather than a narrative, revealing a different learned genre.

variants.name: Ynglinga saga (euhemeristic version)
variants.summary: The gods are historicized as migrating chieftains from Asia (Tyrkland) whose skill in magic won them worship — Snorri's learned-Christian cover story that makes mythology into dynastic history and protects the pagan learning from condemnation.

title.en: Ragnarok: The Doom of the Gods and the Green World After
title.zh: 諸神黃昏：神之劫難與劫後新綠

region.en: Vigríðr plain / Ginnungagap (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland — manuscript provenance)
region.zh: 維格利德戰場／金倫加鴻溝（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利——抄本產地）

texts.period: Voluspa's eschatology c. 900-1000 CE (with debated Christian-era influence); Snorri's systematization c. 1220-1230; principal MSS: Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to (c. 1270s); Codex Regius of the Prose Edda GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa 39-66; Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Gylfaginning 51-53 (trans. Faulkes, 1987)

summary.en: Brother slays brother, the wolf eats sun and moon, and the fettered powers break loose: Loki sails with corpse-ship Naglfar, Surt burns the world, and the gods die in ordered pairs — Odin to the wolf, Thor to the serpent — before the earth rises green, Baldr returns, and life begins again from two survivors.
summary.zh: 兄弟相殘，狼吞日月，縛者俱脫；洛基率死人指甲所造之船而來，蘇爾特烈火焚世；諸神成對赴死——奧丁亡於狼、托爾與世界蛇同盡；而後大地自海中復升而青，巴德爾復歸，二人從木中重生，新世界開始。

sensitivity.note: Historical literary corpus; see note on Norse creation record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Voluspa 44-45: 'Brothers will fight brothers and sisters' children destroy kinship; it is hard in the world, whoredom of an axe-age, a sword-age, a wind-age, a wolf-age, before the world falls; no man will spare another.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Voluspa 44-45; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Voluspa 56-58: 'The sun turns black, earth sinks in the sea, the hot stars are whirled down from heaven; fire leaps the length of the world, high flame plays against heaven itself.' 'Again the earth rises green from the sea; waterfalls fall, and the eagle flies that hunts for fish over the fells.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Voluspa 56-58; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Anthony Faulkes, Snorri Sturluson: Edda, Everyman, London 1987 (public-domain via Brodeur 1916); Ursula Dronke, The Poetic Edda vol. II, Oxford 1997

narrative.en:
Ragnarok ('the doom of the powers') is not a single tale but a prophecy — the whole eschatology is recited by a dead sibyl whom Odin, in the Voluspa's frame, has raised from the grave to compel her speech ('I know where Odin hid his eye...'). Her vision supplies the beginning, middle, and end of the world's death and rebirth.

SIGNS AND FIMBULWINTER. First the moral order breaks: 'brothers will fight brothers and do brothers' deeds; sisters' sons spoil kinship; hard it is in the world, an axe-age, a sword-age, a wind-age, a wolf-age, before the world falls; no man will spare another' (Voluspa 45). Then the cosmic restraints fail: three winters (Fimbulvetr) follow one another with no summers between; the wolf Skoll swallows the sun, Hati the moon (Snorri, Gylf. 51: 'the wolves will swallow sun and moon, and the stars will vanish'); the earth and mountains shake so that trees are torn up, fetters snap, and the bound powers break free: Loki, and the wolf Fenrir, and (in Snorri) Loki steers the ship Naglfar, 'made of dead men's nails', with the giants. The Midgard-serpent Jormungandr, giant of the sea, rises in fury and drives waves over the land; the sea gushes onto the earth. Surt rides from Muspell first and last, fire burning before and behind him; his sword outshines the sun as they ride over Bifrost, which breaks beneath them ('all the gods and all the ranks of the Einherjar arm themselves'). Heimdallr stands up and blows the Gjallarhorn with all his might; Odin rides to Mimir's well to take counsel for himself and his host; the ash Yggdrasil trembles.

THE BATTLE AT VIGRITHR. On the plain Vigrithr, 'a hundred rasts on each side', the armies meet in the order the sources give as if a litany of paired deaths: Odin goes against the wolf Fenrir, and the wolf swallows him; Odin's son Vidarr, strongest after Thor, avenges him — wearing his one thick sandal (made of the leather scraps faithful shoemakers have given up), he grips the wolf's jaws and tears the throat apart with sword or boot. Thor goes against the Midgard-serpent: Mjollnir crushes the serpent's head, and Thor strides nine paces and falls dead from its venom. Freyr goes against Surt; lacking his sword (given to Skirnir long before), he falls. Týr and the hound Garmr slay each other; Loki and Heimdallr slay each other. Then Surt flings fire over the world: 'the sun turns black, earth sinks in the sea, the hot stars are whirled down from heaven; steam rises and life's fosterer, fire, plays against heaven itself' (Voluspa 56-57) — the earth burns and sinks.

RENEWAL. But the vision does not end in ashes: 'again the earth rises green from the sea; waterfalls fall, and the eagle flies that hunts for fish over the fells' (Voluspa 58). The Aesir meet again at Ithavoll and find in the grass the golden tablets (gullnar taflor) the gods' first race had possessed — the golden age restored. Fields bear fruit unsown. Baldr and Hodr come back from Hel's keeping and dwell in Hropt's (Odin's) victory-homes; Hoenir survives to choose the lots of prophecy; two children of the sun walk the ways of the sky (in Snorri, a daughter of the sun as fair as her mother rides where the sun was). Two human beings, Lif and Lifthrasir ('Life' and 'Striving-for-life'), hide in Hoddmimir's wood (Snorri: in Yggdrasil's keeping, feeding on morning dew); their children people the world. Vafthrudnismal 45 confirms: 'Lif and Lifthrasir will live... in Hoddmimir's holt; morning dews they have for food.' There is a hall brighter than the sun, Gimle, roofed with gold, where righteous people shall dwell 'and enjoy delight ever after' (Voluspa 64) — and one 'more powerful than all', who comes from above to judge (the sentence 'then there may come the mighty one, the strong one above, who rules over all' — hinn rikki — has fueled a century of debate between pre-Christian eschatology and post-conversion editing). The sibyl closes on a last grim chord: a dragon, Nidhoggr, flies from Nidafjoll bearing corpses in his feathers — 'now she will sink' — the vision's end and the poem's return to the grave.

FUNCTIONS. Ragnarok gives Norse myth its tragic teleology: the gods know their fate and fight anyway — the ethics of doomed courage (drengskapr) at the center of skaldic ideology; the imagery structures the sagas' battle-scenes, the iconography of the Gosforth (Cumbria) and Thorwald (Man) crosses, and the modern reception of 'twilight of the gods' (Wagner's Gotterdammerung); its 'new earth' stanza is the classic test-case for Christian influence on the eddic corpus.
narrative.zh: 預言之女於奧丁喚起之下，詠世界之終：兄弟相殘，姊妹之子毀親，斧劍風狼之世，世將傾覆。三冬連綿無夏，斯科爾吞日、哈提吞月，群星隕落；大地動搖，枷鎖斷裂——洛基脫縛，駛死人指甲所造之納吉爾法船；耶夢加得巨蛇怒起，海水氾濫陸地；蘇爾特持炎劍自穆斯貝爾海姆驅馳，彩虹橋焚裂。海姆達爾吹加拉爾號角，諸神聚於維格利德平原，百由旬之闊。成對赴死：芬里爾吞奧丁，維達爾裂其顎以復仇；托爾以妙爾尼爾碎蛇首，行九步而亡於毒；弗雷無劍而歿；提爾與加姆同盡；洛基與海姆達爾互斃。蘇爾特舉火焚世：日黑地沉，烈焰沖天，大地沒於海。而後復起：『大地復自海中升起，綠意重生；瀑布飛落，蒼鷹捕魚於山間』。諸神重聚伊達平原，草中尋得金塔羅牌；巴德爾與霍德爾自冥府歸還；生命與生命之欲於霍德密米爾林中食晨露而生，子孫繁衍；金頂吉姆列殿中義人永享安樂。女巫末言：黑龍尼德霍格自尼達山飛來，羽負屍骸——『今我將沉』。功能：以宿命而勇戰為北歐武德之核；石雕十字架與薩迦戰場敘事皆其影像；『諸神黃昏』為基督教影響爭論之試金石。

functions: Tragic teleology: gods fight knowing doom — the ethic of doomed courage (drengskapr)
Iconographic program of the Gosforth and Thorwald crosses and later reception (Wagner's Gotterdammerung)
Renewal eschatology: golden tablets, unsown fields, and the green earth as world-renewal template
Conversion-era debate: the 'mighty one above' as the test-case for Christian influence

variants.name: Voluspa (Poetic Edda)
variants.text_tradition: Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, st. 39-66 (with Hauksbok variants)
variants.summary: The oldest coherent eschatology: moral collapse, wolf-age, paired deaths, Surt's fire, the green earth, Baldr's return, Gimle, and the ambiguous 'mighty one'; closes with the sibyl sinking back into the earth.

variants.name: Snorri's Gylfaginning 51-53
variants.summary: Systematizes the prophecy into prose narrative: names the wolves Skoll and Hati, makes Loki the steersman of Naglfar, gives Vidarr his one-sandale revenge, places Lif and Lifthrasir in Yggdrasil, and adds the sun-daughter — a rationalizing, euhemerism-ready retelling.

variants.name: Vafthrudnismal 39-53
variants.summary: In the wisdom contest, the giant confirms the wolf swallowing Odin and Vidarr's revenge, names the survivors of the gods (Vidar and Vali dwell at Ithavoll where the gods' sanctuaries burn), and locates Lif and Lifthrasir — an independent poetic witness older than Snorri's prose.

variants.name: Baldrs draumar (Poetic Edda)
variants.summary: A narrative prelude: Odin rides to Hel's gate and raises a dead volva to learn why Baldr dreams evil — the prophecy that sets the doom in motion; attests the sibyl-raising motif as story rather than frame.

variants.name: Conversion-era readings (Christian influence debate)
variants.text_tradition: Scholarly controversy: Dronke 1997; McKinnell 2008; Meulengracht Sorensen 1986
variants.summary: The 'green earth' and 'mighty one above' stanzas are variously read as native eschatology, post-conversion interpolation, or a bilingual hybrid; the debate is the standard case study in how myth texts encode conversion.

primary_sources.citation: Stanzas 39-66 (eschatology and renewal); principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to (c. 1270s), with Hauksbok 575 a 4to variant readings. Critical edition: Ursula Dronke, The Poetic Edda vol. II, Oxford 1997.
Chs. 51-53 (doom and renewal). Critical edition: Anthony Faulkes, London 1987; MSS: Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Upsaliensis DG 11 4to. Public-domain English: Brodeur 1916.
